# Imagery standards

Imagery in published writing carries the same honesty obligations as prose, and a
chart can mislead faster than a paragraph. These standards keep the visual layer as
checkable as the evidence layer.

Charts show the measurement, not the impression. Axes start at zero unless a zoomed
range is explicitly labeled as zoomed, with the full-range version linked. Every
chart states its denominator and measurement window in the caption, because a chart
divorced from its caption will travel alone on social channels.

Comparisons plot the same metric for every series, measured the same way over the
same window. A chart comparing our measured number against a competitor's marketing
claim is a category error and does not ship, however the labels hedge it.

Screenshots of product or data are taken from synthetic demonstration environments,
never from customer accounts, and the synthetic environment's data is reviewed for
accidental realism — names, addresses, and figures that could be mistaken for a real
customer's — before capture.

Decorative imagery is minimal and never load-bearing: if removing an image changes
what the reader believes, the image was making a claim, and claims belong in prose
where the evidence standards can reach them. Diagrams that explain mechanisms are
encouraged, drawn from the piece's own vocabulary, and versioned with the piece so a
correction updates both.

## Accessibility

Every published image carries alt text that states what the image shows and, for
charts, the finding the chart carries — a reader who cannot see the chart still gets
the claim and its denominator. Color is never the only channel encoding a series.
